problems.stem: You want to treat learner reflections as data about your design. Which reflection excerpt is analytic enough to code as evidence rather than mere description?
options: I liked the lesson and learned a lot.
When the narration and the on-screen text repeated each other, I stopped reading and just listened, so I missed the labels.
It was a good experience overall.
problems.explanation: Reflection becomes usable data when it names a specific design feature, a behavior, and a consequence. Global praise cannot be coded against a design decision.

problems.stem: To treat reflections as data, you build a small coding scheme. Which code is defined well enough to apply consistently?
options: Redundancy-noticed: the learner reports that narration and on-screen text duplicated each other.
problems.explanation: A codeable category names an observable claim in the text so two coders could agree. Vague valence labels invite inconsistent coding.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to help analyze a set of learner reflections. Which use keeps the analysis trustworthy?
options: Let the AI assign a satisfaction score to each reflection and report it as the finding.
Ask the AI to suggest candidate codes, then you apply the codebook yourself and spot-check the AI's tags against the raw text.
Have the AI summarize the reflections into one upbeat paragraph for the report.
Ask the AI to predict what learners would have said.
problems.explanation: The AI can propose codes, but coding decisions and verification against the source text stay with the analyst. Inventing scores or predicted responses fabricates evidence.

problems.stem: Many reflections say learners felt the simulation "helped them learn." What can you responsibly claim from that pattern?
options: The simulation caused measurable learning gains.
Learners perceived the simulation as helpful, which is a self-report signal worth pairing with a performance measure before claiming a learning effect.
The simulation is effective for all future learners.
problems.explanation: Reflection is self-report, evidence of perception, not of measured learning. Treating felt helpfulness as proven gain overstates what the data shows.
